strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: evaluating and improving video MLLMs for fine-grained human action recognition, especially in egocentric settings where temporal order, object interactions, and subtle action distinctions matter.

The proposed EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA reformulation is useful and well motivated. Using action-recognition models to mine hard distractors exposes a real weakness of current MLLMs that is hidden by random multiple-choice options.
The empirical results on EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA are strong in absolute terms, with large gains over LLaVA-Video and GPT-4o under the reported hard-distractor setting.

The paper includes several relevant ablations, including distractor source, egocentric prompting, temporal detection, vision supervision, GPT-4o distillation, direct prediction, and prior-action memory.
The work compares against both open-source video MLLMs and specialized action recognition models, and it also evaluates transfer to several additional video benchmarks.

The discussion of official EPIC-KITCHENS action keys versus raw narrations is insightful; the paper makes a plausible case that compressed verb-noun labels can be semantically ambiguous for language-based models.
weaknesses: The main methodological contribution is a collection of relatively simple training and prompting additions rather than a clearly unified or technically deep algorithm. Most of the improvement appears to come from fine-tuning on hard multiple-choice distractors, while several proposed components have small or inconsistent marginal effects.

The EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA benchmark has a circularity/fairness concern: hard options are generated by specialized action-recognition models, and the training procedure also uses predictions from similar models. Although the paper distinguishes AVION-trained OOD from TIM-tested OOD, the setup still strongly ties evaluation to the candidate-generation procedure rather than open-ended action understanding.

The comparison to GPT-4o is not fully convincing. GPT-4o is evaluated only with 8 frames due to cost, while the best proposed models use 16 or more frames in several settings. This weakens the headline claim of outperforming GPT-4o by 21 points.

The claimed state-of-the-art result on original EPIC-KITCHENS-100 is hard to interpret. The method appears to use TIM top-K predictions as candidate options, making it closer to reranking/refinement than standard closed-set action classification. The paper does not make the fairness of this comparison sufficiently clear.

Several evaluation choices need stronger justification: why K=5 for the proposed benchmark but K=20 for EPIC-KITCHENS-100, whether the ground-truth answer is always present in candidate sets at test time, and how performance changes under different candidate-generation models or numbers of distractors.

The additional benchmark results are modest and mixed. Improvements over LLaVA-Video-7B are often small, the model is worse on NextQA, and subcategory tables show many regressions. This limits the strength of the generalization claim.

The ablation evidence is somewhat inconsistent. For example, cumulative ablations suggest vision supervision adds several points, but leave-one-out removal from the full model changes performance very little. This makes it difficult to assess which components are truly important.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript text. It states that code and models are available, but the visible manuscript does not provide a concrete URL, and many implementation details of data construction, option sampling, and benchmark release format would be needed to reproduce the exact evaluation.
The benchmark is restricted to EPIC-KITCHENS-style egocentric kitchen actions. This is a meaningful domain, but the paper sometimes frames the conclusions more broadly than the evidence supports.

The writing is generally clear, but the contribution boundaries could be sharper: benchmark construction, candidate reranking, instruction-tuning data augmentation, and action-recognition improvements are interleaved in a way that makes the central scientific claim less crisp.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: evaluating and improving MLLMs for fine-grained egocentric action recognition, where current video MLLMs are plausibly overestimated by easy multiple-choice distractors.

The proposed EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA construction is a useful diagnostic idea. Using action-recognition models to mine hard distractors clearly makes the evaluation harder than random answer choices, as shown by the large drops for GPT-4o and LLaVA baselines.

The empirical study is fairly broad: the paper reports zero-shot baselines, cumulative and leave-one-out ablations, validation results on EPIC-KITCHENS-100, and transfer results on several video QA benchmarks.

The main training recipe produces large gains on the proposed MQA benchmark, especially from training with adversarial distractors, suggesting that hard-negative multiple-choice supervision is practically useful.
weaknesses: The main claims are overstated relative to the evaluation. Much of the reported success is on a newly constructed multiple-choice benchmark where the answer is guaranteed to be among five candidate narrations, so it does not establish robust open-vocabulary action recognition by MLLMs.

The EPIC-KITCHENS-100 SOTA comparison is not fully convincing. The method appears to rely on TIM top-20 candidates at test time and acts partly as a reranker, which is not directly comparable to prior action classifiers over the full label space. The GT narration setting is also not the official evaluation target.

The comparison to GPT-4o is potentially unfair and overemphasized. GPT-4o is evaluated only with 8 frames due to cost, while the main model is reported with more favorable settings elsewhere; moreover, GPT-4o is not fine-tuned on the benchmark-specific format or distractor distribution.

Novelty is limited. The key ingredients, hard-negative mining, auxiliary supervision, GPT-4o distillation, direct prediction, prompt perspective changes, and using prior actions, are mostly incremental combinations of existing ideas rather than a clear new technical contribution.

The ablations weaken the case for several proposed components. The leave-one-out table suggests most additions beyond adversarial distractor training have very small effects, while the cumulative table is confounded by ordering and does not isolate interactions cleanly.

Generalization evidence is modest. Improvements on external benchmarks are small, one benchmark decreases, and the subcategory tables show mixed effects, including drops on several action-related categories.

The benchmark construction may encode biases of the specialist models used to create distractors. The paper does not sufficiently analyze whether performance reflects genuine video understanding versus learning to discriminate among the error modes and candidate distributions of AVION/TIM.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract has an unfinished code/model availability line, and important details such as exact candidate construction, prompts, data release status, scoring/parsing choices, and benchmark files would need to be made precise for reliable replication.

The paper would benefit from stronger error analysis. It shows a few qualitative examples but does not systematically analyze remaining failures, ambiguity in narrations, annotation noise, candidate-set artifacts, or whether models exploit language priors among the options.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely question: whether video MLLMs genuinely recognize fine-grained human actions, especially under visually and semantically confusable alternatives.

The EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA reformulation is well motivated. Using specialist action-recognition models to mine hard distractors is a practical and compelling way to expose weaknesses that random multiple-choice options hide.

Empirical results on the proposed benchmark are strong: fine-tuning LLaVA-Video/OneVision variants with hard distractors and auxiliary tasks yields large gains over zero-shot open-source baselines and GPT-4o under the reported 8-frame setting.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses, including random vs AVION vs TIM distractors, egocentric prompting, leave-one-out component ablations, official keys vs narrations, and transfer to several video benchmarks.

The work is practically relevant: it offers a clear recipe for improving MLLMs on action understanding, and the use of narrations rather than compressed verb-noun labels is a valuable observation for future benchmark design.
weaknesses: The main methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the final system combines fine-tuning on hard multiple-choice examples, auxiliary temporal/direct-prediction tasks, GPT-4o distillation, vision-token supervision, and prior-action context, rather than introducing a clearly new model or learning principle.

The strongest EPIC-KITCHENS-100 result is partly a reranking/refinement setup using TIM top-K predictions, including K=20 for the original benchmark. This makes the SOTA comparison less clean than a standalone action-recognition model and should be framed more carefully.

The proposed benchmark is derived from the EPIC-KITCHENS validation split and uses TIM-generated hard negatives; although AVION negatives are used for OOD training, the evaluation still risks being shaped by the failure modes and label space of the same family of specialist action-recognition systems.

Claims of outperforming GPT-4o are not fully airtight: GPT-4o is evaluated only with 8 frames due to cost, while the best open-source numbers often use more frames and task-specific fine-tuning on the benchmark domain.

The additional benchmark gains are modest and mixed. Improvements over LLaVA-Video-7B are often small, NextQA decreases, and VideoMME action-recognition/action-reasoning subcategories slightly decrease, limiting the strength of the generalization claim.

The leave-one-out ablations weaken some proposed-component claims: vision supervision, GPT-4o distillation, and direct prediction contribute little in the full model despite being emphasized as key methods.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the manuscript: the abstract says code/models are available but no actual link is shown in the extracted text, and there is limited reporting of seeds, variance, statistical significance, or sensitivity to distractor generation choices.

The evaluation would be stronger with more comparisons to specialist video/action models in the exact MQA/reranking setting and with held-out datasets beyond kitchen egocentric videos to test whether the hard-negative training transfers robustly.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap: fine-grained action understanding in video MLLMs, especially beyond easy randomly sampled multiple-choice settings.

The hard-distractor EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA benchmark is a useful diagnostic idea and convincingly shows that random-choice evaluation substantially overestimates current MLLM action recognition ability.

Empirical evaluation is broad: the paper reports results on the proposed benchmark, standard EPIC-KITCHENS action recognition, additional action datasets, multiple general video MLLM benchmarks, and several ablations.
The method is practical and modular: hard distractor training, action-token supervision, temporal detection/order tasks, and two-stage reranking can be applied to several base MLLMs and domains.
Ablations support the main design choices, especially the contribution of adversarial distractor training and the action-token supervision.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is moderate. Hard example mining, auxiliary classification tokens, supervised instruction tuning, and reranking with a specialist model are sensible combinations, but individually familiar.

The strongest action-recognition claims depend on a two-stage pipeline that uses a specialist action-recognition model to generate candidate actions at inference. This makes the comparison to standalone specialist models less clean, since LLaV Action is partly reranking another model's predictions rather than solving the full structured action task independently.

Benchmark and training construction are closely coupled to EPIC-KITCHENS and to specialist-model error distributions. Although the paper discusses AVION-vs-TIM as OOD, the benchmark may still reward models trained to discriminate among specialist-proposed confusions rather than general fine-grained action understanding.

The 'action narration' setting for EPIC-KITCHENS appears less comparable to standard action-label classification, since natural narrations can contain richer instance-specific language and may make the task easier than predicting canonical labels.

General video benchmark gains over LLaVA-Video-7B are mostly small, with some regressions, so the evidence for broad MLLM improvement is weaker than the evidence for the proposed hard MQA/action-recognition setting.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially 'SOTA' framing and the implication that the model strongly generalizes beyond the training domain. The additional domains are useful but still rely on task-specific hard-example construction and/or finetuning.

Reproducibility is not fully established in the manuscript as presented: the abstract says code/data/models are available but the link is missing, and several implementation details for candidate generation and narration selection would need to be very precise to reproduce the main numbers.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: fine-grained action understanding in video MLLMs, especially for egocentric actions where existing general-purpose MLLMs are weak.

The hard-distractor construction for EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA is a reasonable and useful idea; using specialist model confusions produces a more diagnostic evaluation than random multiple-choice options.
The empirical section is broad, covering EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA, standard action recognition datasets, several MLLM benchmarks, ablations, and some qualitative/attention analysis.
The authors provide useful ablations showing that hard distractor training is the dominant contributor, with smaller gains from action token supervision and auxiliary reformulations.
weaknesses: The central performance claims are not fully convincing because the strongest gains largely come from training on reformulated in-domain EPIC-KITCHENS data with hard options generated by action-recognition models. This makes it hard to separate genuine general action understanding from learning the benchmark/task distribution.

The two-stage structured action pipeline depends on an external specialist action recognizer to propose top-K candidates. Claims of SOTA action recognition by the MLLM are therefore overstated: the system inherits recall and biases from the specialist model, and comparisons to standalone action recognition models are not clean.

The benchmark construction and training pipeline are closely coupled. Even when AVION distractors are used for training and TIM for evaluation, both are specialist models trained for the same dataset/task family, so the claimed OOD setting is weak and does not rule out overfitting to specialist-model confusions.

Novelty is limited. Hard negative mining, multiple-choice reformulation, auxiliary classification tokens, and instruction tuning are all familiar ingredients; the contribution is mostly an engineering combination rather than a clearly new modeling or learning principle.

Several evaluations are difficult to interpret. The “action narration” setting appears non-standard and may not be comparable to conventional action-label classification; the paper should more clearly define how candidate narrations are selected and whether any instance-specific information leaks into evaluation.

Results on broader MLLM benchmarks are modest: improvements over LLaVA-Video-7B are often small, mixed, or negative, which weakens the claim that the method broadly improves action/video understanding rather than improving the constructed EPIC-style task.

The action token analysis is suggestive but not decisive. Attention/correlation statistics do not establish that the token causes better visual grounding, and the action-token contribution is small in the leave-one-out ablation compared with hard distractor training.

The paper’s framing is frequently stronger than the evidence supports, especially around “fair” comparison to specialist models, generalization, and MLLMs as a path forward for structured action recognition.

strengths: Strong, well-motivated contribution: the paper exposes weaknesses in MLLM fine-grained action understanding using specialist-model hard distractors rather than easy random choices.
Broad and convincing empirical evaluation across EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA, standard action recognition benchmarks, Animal Kingdom, and general video-MLLM benchmarks.

Good ablation coverage, including additive and leave-one-out studies that clarify the roles of adversarial distractors, temporal detection, direct prediction, temporal order learning, and the action token.
The AVION-training/TIM-testing setup is a thoughtful attempt to reduce overfitting to the benchmark distractor generator.
The method is practical and likely useful to the community, with promised release of code, data, benchmarks, models, prompts, and licensing details.
weaknesses: The benchmark and training recipe are still closely coupled through specialist-model distractors, so some gains may reflect adaptation to candidate distributions rather than general action understanding.
The two-stage structured action prediction pipeline depends on an external action-recognition model at inference, complicating claims of standalone SOTA action recognition.
Some comparisons are not perfectly controlled: frame counts differ, GPT-4o is evaluated only at 8 frames, and downstream experiments use dataset-specific candidate generators or finetuning.
Using action narrations as answer options is reasonable for MLLMs but may introduce annotation-style or lexical cues; stronger text-only controls would help.
The attention analysis is only suggestive and does not causally establish improved use of visual evidence.
The ethics statement is brief for a human behavior understanding system and should discuss surveillance, consent, and misuse risks more fully.
